title: Small Stock Pre-slaughter and Slaughter Procedures (including Stunning, Lifting, Throat Cutting, and Bleeding)

lessons.title: Before slaughter: receiving, resting and inspection
lessons.html:
Receiving sheep and goats

  1. Check the documents: owner, number of animals, and proof of ownership.
  2. Count the animals as they come off the truck.
  3. Look at each animal. Report dead, injured, lame or sick animals to the supervisor and meat inspector.
  4. Off-load calmly. Never throw, drag or kick animals.

The lairage

  • Put animals in clean pens. Do not overcrowd.
  • Give clean water in every pen.
  • Let animals rest before slaughter, for the time your plant procedure sets. Rested animals bleed better and give better meat.
  • Keep the pen number, owner and count on the lairage record.

Ante-mortem inspection

The meat inspector looks at the animals in the pens before slaughter. This is ante-mortem inspection. The inspector looks for animals that are sick, injured or not fit for slaughter.

  • Healthy animals go to normal slaughter.
  • Suspect animals go to a separate pen and may be slaughtered separately at the end of the day.
  • Some animals may be rejected.

Never slaughter an animal the inspector has set aside without the inspector's permission.

Clean animals

Very dirty or wet animals carry more germs into the abattoir. Report very dirty animals. Wet wool is hard to handle hygienically; follow your plant procedure for wet animals.

Moving to the stunning area

Move small groups quietly through the race. Sheep follow each other. Do not rush them or use force.

lessons.title: Stunning and lifting
lessons.html:
Why we stun

Stunning makes the animal unconscious so it feels no pain during throat cutting and bleeding. It must stay unconscious until it dies from loss of blood. Only trained, authorised workers may stun.

Stunning methods for small stock

  • Electrical stunning (head-only): tongs are placed on both sides of the head so current passes through the brain. This is the most common method for sheep and lambs.
  • Captive bolt: often used for goats, rams with heavy horns, or as a back-up stunner.

The settings and the correct position are set by your abattoir. Follow the procedure. Do not change settings.

Doing it right

  1. Check the stunner works before the shift, and that the back-up stunner is ready.
  2. Restrain the animal in the restrainer or stunning pen.
  3. Place the tongs firmly in the correct position, or place the captive bolt correctly on the head.
  4. Apply for the full time the procedure says.

Signs of an effective stun

  • Immediate collapse.
  • No rhythmic breathing.
  • No blinking when the eye is touched.
  • No attempt to lift the head.

If any sign of waking appears, stun again at once with the back-up stunner and tell the supervisor.

Lifting (hoisting)

Straight after stunning, put a shackle on one hind leg and hoist the animal onto the bleeding rail. Work quickly so that the time from stunning to bleeding stays short, as your plant procedure sets.

Safety

Stunned animals kick. Keep your face and body away from the legs. Keep cables dry and report damage.

lessons.title: Throat cutting and bleeding
lessons.html:
Throat cutting (sticking)

The throat is cut to cut the main blood vessels in the neck so that blood drains quickly and the animal dies without waking up.

  1. Use a sharp, clean, sterilised knife.
  2. Make the cut as you were trained: across the throat or by a chest stick that cuts the main vessels near the heart, according to your plant's method.
  3. Cut quickly and completely. A slow or incomplete cut gives poor bleeding.
  4. Put the knife in the sterilizer before the next animal.

In abattoirs approved for religious slaughter, trained slaughtermen follow the approved procedure under supervision. Welfare rules still apply.

Bleeding

  • Let the animal bleed for the full time your plant sets before the next step.
  • Check that the animal is dead before work starts on the feet, head and skin. Never start dressing an animal that shows signs of life.
  • Blood runs into the bleeding trough. Keep blood off the floor and walkways as far as possible.

Why good bleeding matters

  • Meat with blood left in it looks dark and spoils faster.
  • Good bleeding is a sign that stunning and sticking were done well.

Hygiene at the bleeding area

  • The outside of the animal is dirty. Wash hands and sterilise the knife often.
  • Do not let the head or wool touch other animals on the rail.

Safety

  • Cut away from your body and your other hand.
  • Wear your cut-resistant glove if provided.
  • Stand to the side of kicking legs.

Key points

  • Check, count and inspect animals on arrival; give them water and rest.
  • Never slaughter an animal the meat inspector has set aside.
  • Stun so the animal is unconscious; re-stun at once if it shows signs of waking.
  • Hoist and bleed quickly after stunning.
  • Sterilise the knife after every animal.
  • Never start dressing an animal that shows signs of life.
